title: Accounting & Reporting Considerations for Public Market Readiness
summary: Explore key accounting and reporting considerations for companies preparing to enter the public markets.
body_markdown:
Public-market readiness extends far beyond the transaction itself. As companies move closer to an IPO or other public market event, they begin to face a new set of expectations around financial reporting, accounting, governance, and regulatory compliance. The ability to produce accurate, auditable financial information and support it with robust processes often becomes a key factor in determining whether a transaction proceeds smoothly or encounters costly delays.


In the[first phase of IPO readiness](https://www.cbiz.com/insights/article/ipo-readiness-begins-before-the-market-window-opens) , companies should focus on establishing audit readiness, organizing diligence materials, and developing a strong operating story for investors. Phase two shifts the focus from preparation to execution, requiring management to evaluate whether its accounting policies, internal controls, reporting processes, and finance organization can withstand the scrutiny of auditors, regulators, and public-market investors.


Now, we’ll explore the accounting and reporting considerations that become increasingly important as companies approach the public markets. From revenue recognition, stock-based compensation, and[PCAOB audits](https://www.cbizcpas.com/services/sec-pcaob-financial-audits) to internal controls, SEC reporting, and board oversight, these areas help determine whether a company is prepared not only to complete a transaction but also to operate successfully as a public company from day one.


## Start with Audit Readiness


Before a company can become IPO-ready, it must first become audit-ready. Public-market transactions depend on reliable financial reporting, and that begins with the ability to produce complete, supportable financial statements that can withstand a PCAOB audit.


Many private companies discover weaknesses in their accounting processes only when preparing for a transaction. Documentation may be incomplete, accounting positions may not be fully supported, or financial reporting may rely too heavily on manual processes and institutional knowledge. Addressing these issues early can help prevent delays once auditors, regulators, and investors become involved.


Companies should also begin operating with a public-company mindset before a transaction is imminent. Disciplined close processes, timely reporting, and documented accounting judgments can help identify gaps while there is still time to address them.


## Address Accounting Issues Early


Several accounting areas consistently receive heightened attention during the path to the public markets. Revenue recognition is often among the most significant. Contract terms, performance obligations, pricing arrangements, and customer incentives can all affect how and when revenue is recognized. Management should ensure accounting policies are aligned with current guidance and supported by contract language.


Stock-based compensation is another common area of scrutiny. Equity issued before a public-market transaction may require detailed valuation analysis, particularly when grant-date values differ significantly from an anticipated offering price. Companies should maintain robust support for equity valuations and document the assumptions behind those conclusions.


Other areas that frequently require technical accounting analysis include business combinations, fair value measurements, income taxes, and significant estimates. Preparing technical accounting memoranda before the audit process begins can help support management’s conclusions and reduce surprises later.


## Strengthen Controls, Processes, and Systems


Going public introduces reporting expectations that many private-company processes were never designed to support. Investors and regulators expect financial information to be timely, accurate, and backed by effective internal controls.


Management should evaluate controls over financial reporting, approval processes, segregation of duties, system access, and documentation practices. Growing companies often rely on spreadsheets and manual reviews that become increasingly difficult to manage as reporting obligations expand.


Technology also plays an important role. Accounting systems should provide reliable audit trails and support repeatable reporting processes. Automating key activities can improve efficiency while reducing the risk of errors.


Although Sarbanes-Oxley compliance requirements may not apply immediately to every company, organizations should begin assessing their control environment well before a transaction. Building controls after going public is often more costly and disruptive than addressing gaps beforehand.


## Prepare for Public-Company Reporting


A successful transaction is only the beginning. Public companies face ongoing obligations that require a different level of discipline and coordination than most private organizations are accustomed to.


Management should assess whether its finance team has the experience and capacity to support quarterly and annual reporting, SEC filings, technical accounting requirements, and disclosure obligations. In some cases, additional internal resources may be necessary. In others, external advisors can help bridge knowledge or staffing gaps during the transition.


Companies should also begin thinking about how they will communicate financial performance to investors. One of the most important components of that process is Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A).


An effective MD&A goes beyond explaining what happened during the reporting period. It helps investors understand why results changed, what factors drove performance, and which metrics management uses to evaluate the business. Rather than repeating information already contained in the financial statements, the MD&A should provide context that helps readers understand the story behind the numbers.


## Effective Governance Matters


As organizations approach the public markets, governance becomes increasingly important. Investors, exchanges, and regulators expect companies to have appropriate oversight structures in place, including a qualified board of directors and audit committee.


Building that structure should begin well before a transaction is underway. Board members with relevant financial, industry, or public-company experience can help management navigate reporting requirements, governance expectations, and strategic decisions throughout the process.


The goal is not simply to satisfy a listing requirement. Effective governance can improve decision-making, strengthen accountability, and enhance credibility with investors. Companies should focus on finding directors whose experience aligns with their business, growth strategy, and long-term objectives.


## Readiness Beyond the Transaction


Whether a company pursues a traditional IPO, direct listing, de-SPAC transaction, or another path to the public markets, the underlying expectations remain largely the same. Investors and regulators expect reliable financial reporting, strong governance, effective controls, and transparent disclosures.


Often, the companies that begin preparing early for going public are the most successful. By addressing accounting issues early, strengthening reporting processes, documenting key judgments, and building the right team of advisors and leaders, organizations can position themselves to respond when opportunities arise.


Ultimately, going public is not just a financing event. It is a transition to operating under a new level of scrutiny and accountability. Companies that build the necessary accounting and reporting infrastructure in advance are better positioned to complete the transaction efficiently and operate with confidence as a public company.
